parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Choose what the center should own
parts.body:
An AI operating model decides which work is shared and who owns each deployed outcome. Centralization can make scarce expertise and controls available across the enterprise, but a central team that builds and approves every workflow will accumulate a queue. Federation puts decisions close to business context, but each unit may duplicate platforms or apply uneven standards. A hybrid model often gives a central group common platform, risk methods, evaluation tools, and portfolio visibility while business or product teams own workflows, adoption, and results. These are design options, not a universal org chart.

Draw the boundary around recurring decisions. Who can select a provider, grant access to sensitive data, change a prompt or model, approve customer release, accept residual risk, and turn a system off? Assign one accountable owner for each, then name required reviewers and the evidence they need. A central platform may set a supported model list; a business team still decides whether a specific assistant improves its service. Security retains its established authority over security controls.

Use workload and risk to select the model. If only a few teams can operate AI safely, central specialist delivery may be a temporary bridge. As capabilities grow, move workflow decisions toward domain teams with shared guardrails. Revisit the boundary when central queues grow or local incidents reveal uneven practice.

example.title: A useful split
example.body: For a customer assistant, the central platform owns identity integration, logging, and an approved model gateway. The service product leader owns the experience, fallback, benefits, and incident contact. Data stewardship decides the permitted source and access rules; security and privacy exercise their control duties. The CAIO maintains common evaluation requirements and portfolio review.

exercise.title: Map six decisions
exercise.body: For one use case, list provider selection, data access, evaluation criteria, release, incident response, and retirement. Give each one decision maker, reviewers, an evidence artifact, and an escalation route. Identify any row with duplicate approvers or no owner.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: governance roles and responsibilities

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Make the interface between teams explicit
parts.body:
A hybrid model fails at the handoff if local teams cannot tell what the central function supplies. Publish a service catalogue: supported models and data patterns, evaluation templates, access request route, incident contact, and expected response times. State what local teams must bring: a business owner, intended population, data classification, baseline, evaluation cases, and an operating plan. Avoid treating an approved model as blanket approval for every use of it.

Define change classes. A wording correction in a low-risk internal aid may follow local testing and logging. A new sensitive data source, external audience, or autonomous action needs another review by the appropriate owners. The specific thresholds belong in company policy and applicable law. The center should record exceptions and recurring friction. If every project requests the same exception, repair the shared service or the rule rather than negotiating indefinitely.

Document the funding arrangement as well. A central platform has shared costs; local teams have product and review costs. Allocate them transparently so business sponsors do not mistake subsidized infrastructure for a profitable use case.

example.title: One request, two owners
example.body: A claims team asks to add a new repository. Its product owner describes the use and tests retrieval quality. The data steward determines whether the repository may be used and who can see it. Platform engineering implements access controls. The release record names the accountable claims executive and the reviewers' decisions.

exercise.title: Write a service contract
exercise.body: Draft a one-page interface between central AI enablement and a product team. Include the intake evidence, what the central service delivers, the review trigger for a material change, the escalation deadline, and how shared cost appears in the product case.

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Put authority near the incident
parts.body:
The ownership table must work during an outage or harmful output. A product owner should know how to disable the user-facing function or route people to the previous workflow. Platform operations should know how to disable a shared model or revoke credentials. Security and privacy teams handle events within their respective authority. Escalation criteria specify when the incident commander, legal counsel, and senior executive join. A CAIO coordinates AI-specific evidence across products without becoming the only person able to press stop.

Practice an incident: an assistant exposes a document from the wrong customer account. Who suspends access in minutes? Who determines scope from logs? Who informs affected parties under the applicable obligations? Who decides when service may resume? Canada and EU operations may have different reporting and privacy duties, so legal and privacy owners should map the applicable requirements for each deployment. The operating model records those owners; it does not invent one worldwide notice rule.

Review queues, exceptions, and incidents each quarter. Track time from request to decision, repeated evaluation defects, local workarounds, and service adoption. If a central control is too slow, revise its process without silently waiving the underlying risk.

example.title: A stop authority
example.body: In an illustrative service, the product on-call lead can disable the assistant immediately; platform operations can revoke its retrieval access; the privacy incident lead assesses disclosure obligations. A restart requires the product owner and control owners to see the root cause, fix, and verification results.

exercise.title: Tabletop the first hour
exercise.body: For the document exposure scenario, write the first five actions, the person authorized for each, what evidence is preserved, and who can approve restart. Check whether any action waits on a single unavailable executive.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: monitoring, incident response, and change management

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Choose a structure for three business units
parts.body:
Imagine three units: a regulated customer service group, an internal operations group, and a small product team. Each wants AI support and has different capacity. A single pattern may be wasteful. The central group can provide a common identity, vendor, evaluation, and incident foundation. The regulated group may need embedded risk and domain specialists; the small team may need hands-on central delivery for a period. Ownership of each business result stays named.

Prepare an operating model decision with a staffing and funding plan. Show the central team's service demand, the local capability each unit must supply, the review path for high impact uses, and how standards can be updated. Define a migration condition: for example, a unit gains authority to release within a defined class after it demonstrates evaluation, monitoring, and incident readiness. Do not imply that delegation transfers the obligations of control owners.

A mature model is visible in decision speed and quality. Measure the time to an evidence-based release decision and the number of incidents or rework events, not merely how many teams have a champion. Ask leaders whether the boundary resolves disputes they actually encounter.

example.title: A phased hybrid
example.body: The central team supplies gateway, logging, evaluation templates, and office hours. The service group hires an AI product lead and domain evaluators. Internal operations gets a coached product owner. The small product team receives temporary engineering help. After two successful releases and an incident drill, each unit's delegated change class is reviewed; these conditions are illustrative.

exercise.title: Defend the operating model
exercise.body: Draw a table for central and three local teams covering platform, use-case selection, data access, evaluation, release, benefit tracking, and incidents. Give the executive sponsor two tradeoffs and a six-month signal that would cause you to shift the boundary.
